title: Basic
full_review:
When a Special Forces training operation in Panama goes bad, a ex-Army Ranger is called in to unravel where the bodies are and what happened in the macho action flick, "Basic" (Columbia).

A muscular and cocky John Travolta dominates most of the scenes as an investigator pressed into service by a former colleague, Col. Styles (Tim Daly). Capt. Osborne (Connie Nielsen) is getting nowhere questioning surviving trainee Dunbar (Brian Van Holt), but resents the presence of Tom Hardy (Travolta), now a DEA agent under suspicion of being dirty.

Dunbar reluctantly spins an ugly tale of how the hated Sgt. West (Samuel L. Jackson) pushed his six trainees to the limit and beyond, dropping them from a chopper in the Panama jungle at night during a hurricane -- and ended up being shot by one of them.

In the angry recriminations that followed among the six, more shots are fired and only Dunbar and a wounded Kendall (Giovanni Ribisi) were rescued, the other bodies having washed away in the storm. The hospitalized Kendall tells a slightly different story, however, incriminating Dunbar. Col. Styles wants it to end there with Dunbar as the culprit, especially since Kendall is the gay son of a general who could ruin Styles' career if his son is ensnared in the scandal.

Osborne however has her doubts, and with Hardy alongside, digs deeper.

In the style of the 1950 film classic, "Rashomon," the different versions of what happened to the sergeant and those under him are seen in fast-paced, nighttime visuals which are replayed with alterations when the survivors' stories change. With nearly a dozen characters to keep track of, and all the murky visuals dished out to numbing effect, the serpentine plot twists, at first interesting and involving, gradually become tedious.

Taye Diggs plays a black trainee first accused of shooting West, and Harry Connick Jr. has a role as a military doctor with questionable ethics, but Travolta carries the brawny movie on his confident shoulders.

Director John McTiernan delivers the action goods proficiently, but the film is so densely plotted that characterizations suffer. Ultimately the plot twists prove unsatisfying and one feels mostly relief when it is all over. Nielsen is unremarkable as the female investigator and her occasional Southern accent only calls attention to itself.

The movie seems more impressed with its own cleverness than with distinguishing among the trainees and beckoning the audience to care about their fates.

While it may find a receptive young male audience, its repetitive shootings and preponderance of assaultive language and profanity make it of much less interest to the Catholic audience.

Because of recurring violence, much rough language and intermittent profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
